result.summary: Jupiter splits the year between Ceres and Pluto, and a cheered Ceres asks Arethusa why she became a spring. Arethusa tells how the river-god Alpheus chased her from Arcadia and how Diana saved her by turning her into a stream that flowed underground to Ortygia.

scenes.title: Ceres questions Arethusa
scenes.summary: After Jupiter divides the year, Proserpina is happy again and Ceres asks Arethusa for her story. Arethusa rises from the fountain to answer.

scenes.title: Bathing in the quiet stream
scenes.summary: Arethusa, a huntress nymph, bathes naked in a clear stream and is startled by the voice of Alpheus. She flees.
scenes.stakes: Her safety and honor, threatened by a pursuing river-god.

scenes.title: The long chase
scenes.summary: Alpheus pursues Arethusa across Arcadia to Elis, and she grows exhausted. She calls on Dictynna for help.
scenes.stakes: Being overtaken and violated by Alpheus.

scenes.title: Cloud, stream and Ortygia
scenes.summary: Diana hides her in a cloud, and Arethusa dissolves into a stream. Alpheus becomes water to join her, but the goddess splits the earth and Arethusa flows to Ortygia.
scenes.stakes: Her life and freedom, as Alpheus waits at the cloud.

alias_notes.explanation: A cult title of Diana, goddess of hunting; the text also calls her the Delian Goddess.
Refers to Diana, born on Delos.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid simile of doves fleeing the hawk captures the chase.
Moment of Arethusa's transformation into a stream.

analysis.text: The story echoes Proserpina's abduction: another female victim of unwanted pursuit is saved by transformation. Metamorphosis serves as escape and loss.
The tale is an aetiological myth explaining the spring Arethusa at Syracuse and a supposed link with the Alpheus river in Greece.

legacy.text: The Arethusa and Alpheus legend inspired later poets, including Shelley's poem Arethusa (1820).

fun_facts.text: Ancient writers claimed objects thrown into the Alpheus in Greece would emerge at Arethusa's spring in Syracuse.

language_notes.text: 'Common Divinity of two kingdoms' means Proserpina is a goddess shared between the upper world and the underworld, spending part of the year in each.
The 'stream of Elis' is Arethusa herself; she was linked with the river Alpheus in Elis, in the Peloponnese, before becoming a Sicilian spring. 'Amours' means love affairs.
Stymphalus was an Arcadian region with a lake and wood, famous for the birds of Hercules' labours. Here it is just a hunting ground.
'Hoary' means grey-white, describing the pale leaves of the willows; 'shelving' means gently sloping.
Alpheus is a river god of Elis who loved Arethusa. His voice comes from the water, so the stream itself is the pursuer.
These are Arcadian and Elean places, so the chase crosses the Peloponnese from north to west, ending at Elis, the region of Alpheus's river.
Fillets are ribbons or bands tied around the hair.
Dictynna is a title of Diana (Greek Artemis), probably linked to hunting nets. Arethusa invokes her mistress as a nymph in her service.
'The river' is Alpheus, who has been a man in pursuit; the narrator names him by his true nature as a river god.
'Delian Goddess' means Diana, born on Delos with her brother Apollo.
Ortygia is an island at Syracuse in Sicily; the name is also linked to Diana's worship. Arethusa surfaces there as a spring.

context_notes.text: Jupiter's brother is Pluto, who abducted Proserpina. Her 'disconsolate sister' is Ceres, Proserpina's mother, who is also Jupiter's sister.
Achaia is a region of Greece. Arethusa describes herself as a follower of Diana, devoted to hunting and avoiding love.
Diana, goddess of hunting and chastity, protects her followers from unwanted pursuit by hiding or transforming them.
Alpheus was a river in Elis. The myth explained why his waters were said to flow under the sea and rise again in Sicily with the spring Arethusa.

literary_notes.text: Proserpina's face brightening is compared to the sun breaking free of rain clouds, which makes the relief visible.
Arethusa's shame at her beauty shows her as modest and uninterested in love, which sets up the irony of being pursued.
The motionless, transparent water creates a calm, inviting scene, so the sudden noise that follows is more startling.
Her undressing and plunging in, unguarded, hints at the vulnerability that Alpheus will exploit.
Alpheus repeats his question, and the hollow tone makes the voice from the water sound eerie and insistent.
Doves fleeing the hawk compare the nymph's terror and the pursuer's predation, reversing the usual image of gentle pursuit.
She wonders whether the shadow is only fear's invention, showing how terror blurs perception.
Arethusa asks what she felt, then answers with the helpless lamb, drawing the listener into her fear.
The motionless hare among hunting dogs conveys her frozen terror while hidden in the cloud.
Her fear-sweat literally becomes water, so the transformation grows naturally out of her bodily terror.
